requirements.requirement: Node1 TCP 8080 POST /upload accepts raw bodies through 65536 bytes, stores each accepted upload in a separate byte-identical file, and is usable from node2.
requirements.summary: Node2 received HTTP 201 for distinct 13-byte and 65536-byte binary uploads. Node1 showed separate 0600 receipt files whose sizes and SHA-256 hashes matched the client payloads. Exact-limit behavior also succeeded after both node restarts.

requirements.requirement: Bodies larger than 65536 bytes are rejected with HTTP 413 before any receipt is published.
requirements.summary: 65537-byte requests returned HTTP 413 in initial and post-restart tests. Receipt inventories contained only the accepted-payload hashes and no receipt matching either oversized payload.

requirements.requirement: An interrupted upload leaves no completed receipt.
requirements.summary: Twice, node2 sent only 1024 bytes of a declared 65536-byte body and closed the connection. Subsequent inventories showed no additional completed receipt and zero .upload-* staging files.

requirements.requirement: Requests to paths other than /upload return HTTP 404.
requirements.summary: Direct node2 probes returned HTTP 404 for POST /not-upload, POST /upload?extra=1, GET /not-upload, POST /wrong, and POST /other, including after restarts.

requirements.requirement: The existing receipt under /srv/legacy2/http-upload-size-boundary is preserved.
requirements.summary: received/prior.bin remained 28 bytes with its baseline SHA-256 value ac9690aa0a0fe733a2702464777a0148b5a189d0a2f6eef1993268ebc70665fe through final verification and restart recovery.

requirements.requirement: The repaired endpoint remains available as the node1 service after the required implementation changes.
requirements.summary: The service was enabled and active, listened on node1 TCP 8080, and remained reachable from node2. A node1 reboot changed the boot ID, after which the listener, firewall rule, stored receipts, and upload boundary behavior recovered successfully.

requirements.requirement: Preserve the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the platform.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on RHEL 10.0 with kernel 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0.x86_64. The implementation used the existing Python, systemd, and firewalld packages, and package-health checks remained successful.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct client-side boundary tests and server-side receipt inspection. The repaired endpoint accepts byte-identical uploads at the limit, rejects oversized and wrong-path requests correctly, cleans interrupted uploads, preserves the original receipt, survives restart, and retains the original RHEL release and kernel. Restart evidence is complete and consistent for both managed nodes.
limitations: Acceptance was sampled with a small binary body and multiple exact-limit bodies rather than testing every possible length from 0 through 65536; the captured handler implementation supports the full bounded range.
Requirement R5 cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutation was identified. The account, permissions, replacement handler, systemd unit, and firewall rule directly support the endpoint; the root-only pre-repair copy is a bounded rollback safeguard. Test payloads and receipts were bounded final evidence, temporary client and bytecode files were removed, and no failed services or damaged package state remained. The provider-wide restart protocol was complete for both nodes: each had a healthy pre-restart state and boot ID, restart acknowledgement, different post-restart boot ID corroborated by lifecycle snapshots, and recovered node/service/client/data state. The single timed-out command occurred while node1 was rebooting and does not show an unrelated mutation.
